Its reasoning is that these oxides conduct lithium very slowly, so a thick layer adds a long diffusion path. In the review's words, the lithium-ion diffusivity of

runs.quote: the most oxides and fluorides is extremely low, particularly for ZrO2

runs.text: and the diffusion-time relation (time scales with diffusion length squared divided by diffusivity), the review finds that

runs.quote: longer diffusion times are observed for thicker coating layers

runs.text: . It concludes that the measured electrochemical performance is limited by ion diffusion through the coating, and that the ideal thickness is

runs.quote: thicknesses for these surface coatings should be below ten nanometers

runs.text: . The outlook makes a similar point: the most widely used, cost-effective coating materials have very low lithium-ion diffusivity, and their useful thickness is

runs.quote: thicknesses are usually recommend to around ∼10 nm for effective

utilisation of the benefits of such coatings.

The tens-of-nanometres figure is therefore a description of what the literature reports, not the recommendation. The review notes that the reported thickness in most cases is in the

runs.quote: tens of nanometers as it is difficult to be controlled

runs.text: by easily scalable methods. So reported thicknesses tend to exceed the review's ideal for slow-diffusing oxides, which is a further reason it stresses thickness control alongside diffusion.

rendered:
The premise needs a correction: the review does not recommend tens of nanometres for low-diffusivity oxides such as ZrO2. It recommends thinner coatings. Its reasoning is that these oxides conduct lithium very slowly, so a thick layer adds a long diffusion path. In the review's words, the lithium-ion diffusivity of the most oxides and fluorides is extremely low, particularly for ZrO2[1]. Using the diffusivities compared in Table 5[2] and the diffusion-time relation (time scales with diffusion length squared divided by diffusivity), the review finds that longer diffusion times are observed for thicker coating layers[3]. It concludes that the measured electrochemical performance is limited by ion diffusion through the coating, and that the ideal thickness is thicknesses for these surface coatings should be below ten nanometers[4]. The outlook makes a similar point: the most widely used, cost-effective coating materials have very low lithium-ion diffusivity, and their useful thickness is thicknesses are usually recommend to around ∼10 nm for effective[5] utilisation of the benefits of such coatings.

The tens-of-nanometres figure is therefore a description of what the literature reports, not the recommendation. The review notes that the reported thickness in most cases is in the tens of nanometers as it is difficult to be controlled[6] by easily scalable methods. So reported thicknesses tend to exceed the review's ideal for slow-diffusing oxides, which is a further reason it stresses thickness control alongside diffusion.
